To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the incidence of myocardial infraction (MI) in HIV-1-inflicted individuals was higher than in the general French population, with an excess risk in women, especially in the period 2000– 2002, and a decreasing trend thereafter.

(1) the absolute rate difference of myocardial infraction (MI) was higher in women than men in 2006-2009; (2) the trends of MI incidence were different between men (decreasing) and women (no change); and (3) the age of MI diagnosis was significantly lower than in the general French population.
The incidence of MI among adults with HIV-1 infection is increasing, but the risk remains elevated only among women and individuals with CD4 counts <500/μL or with detectable viral load on cART.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a specific population of HIV-infected individuals.
the study of the risk factors of myocardial infraction among people living with HIV- 1, the impact of gender and the impact of antiretroviral therapy.
the impact of HIV infection on the risk and trends in the risk of MI in France.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV-1 infection is associated with an increased risk of MI in men, but not in women.
HIV infection is not an independent risk factor for MI in the current era of cART.

the risk of myocardia infarction is not elevated among HIV-1 positive individuals on cART with CD4 >500 and controlled viral-load, but that it is higher in HIV positive women than men, and that the age of myocardia infraction in HIV positive individuals is younger than in the non HIV positive general population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of myocardiac infarction in the HIV-1 population is not different than in the general French population.
the risk for HIV-1 infected individuals is different between men and woman.
the risk of MI is increased in women living with HIV- 1, but not in men.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women living with HIV- 1 have a higher risk of MI than men and that the risk is no longer elevated among individuals on effective ART.
HIV infection is a risk factor for MI in both men and women and that women are more vulnerable to the effect of HIV infection on MI risk.

the risk of MI among individuals living with HIV-2 was no longer elevated in 2006-2009, especially among those with CD4 ≥ 500 cells/μL and a controlled viral load, and that the risk of early-onset MI was significantly higher in women than men.
